care: The Roman lives tell of civil wars, political murders and battles, including the assassination of Julius Caesar and the deaths of Cicero, Antony and Cleopatra. The lesson names these events without detail. Young readers can start with Romulus and Remus, Caesar and the pirates, and Cato the Elder’s plain living.

young.html: The Greek writer Plutarch paired each famous Greek with a famous Roman. His Romans include Romulus, who by legend founded Rome; Cato, a stern old farmer-statesman; Cicero, the great speaker; and Julius Caesar, the general who made himself master of Rome.

One of Plutarch’s stories: when Caesar was a young man, pirates captured his ship and asked for a ransom of twenty talents of silver. Caesar laughed and said he was worth at least fifty. While his friends gathered the money, he lived among the pirates for thirty-eight days, joined their games, made them listen to his poems, and told them to be quiet when he wanted to sleep. Plutarch tells it to show how bold and sure of himself Caesar was, even then.

Small things show character. Plutarch thought little moments tell us who a person is. Think of someone you know well. Write down one small thing they once did or said that shows what they are like: kind, brave, funny, patient. Read it to your family and see if they can guess who it is.

young.cap: Choose a pair: the Greek on top, the Roman below, Plutarch at the bottom.

full.html: Plutarch (c. AD 46–c. 120) wrote his Parallel Lives when Rome ruled the whole Mediterranean. His Romans run from the legendary founders, Romulus and Numa, through the heroes of the early Republic, such as Camillus and Coriolanus, to the men of the last century of the Republic: Marius and Sulla, Pompey and Crassus, Cato the Younger, Cicero, Caesar, Brutus and Antony. Read together, these lives tell how the Republic grew great and then tore itself apart in civil wars.

full.name: gb-parallel-lives
full.cap: Each Roman beside his Greek partner, and Plutarch’s own lifetime for scale.

full.html: Plutarch tells Caesar’s life through vivid moments. Crossing the Alps on his way to govern a province, Caesar passed a poor mountain village, and his companions joked about whether even there men fought to be first.

full.text: To which Cæsar made answer seriously, “For my part, I had rather be the first man among these fellows, than the second man in Rome.”
full.author: Plutarch
full.tr: John Dryden and others, revised by Arthur Hugh Clough
full.ed: The Harvard Classics, vol. 12, P. F. Collier & Son

full.html: Years later, after a lightning campaign in Asia Minor in 47 BC, he reported his victory to a friend in Rome.

full.text: He used three words, I came, saw, and conquered, which in Latin having all the same cadence, carry with them a very suitable air of brevity.
full.author: Plutarch
full.tr: John Dryden and others, revised by Arthur Hugh Clough
full.ed: The Harvard Classics, vol. 12, P. F. Collier & Son

full.html: The three Latin words are veni, vidi, vici. Plutarch, writing in Greek, admires how they sound alike and how short they are: the style matches the speed of the campaign.
And on his last day, in 44 BC:

full.text: One finds it also related by many, that a soothsayer bade him prepare for some great danger on the ides of March. When the day was come, Cæsar, as he went to the senate, met this soothsayer, and said to him by way of raillery, “The ides of March are come;” who answered him calmly, “Yes, they are come, but they are not past.”
full.author: Plutarch
full.tr: John Dryden and others, revised by Arthur Hugh Clough
full.ed: The Harvard Classics, vol. 12, P. F. Collier & Son

full.html: That day a group of senators led by Brutus and Cassius killed Caesar in the senate meeting. Plutarch tells it in several lives (Caesar, Brutus, Cicero, Antony) from different sides, so readers see one event through several characters.

items: Romulus, raised with his twin Remus, by legend, by a she-wolf; he founds Rome (by tradition in 753 BC). Plutarch reports several versions and admits much is fable.
Coriolanus, a proud general who, driven out of Rome, leads an enemy army against it, and turns back only when his mother Volumnia pleads with him.
Cato the Elder, who wore plain clothes, worked in the fields beside his slaves and fought luxury as censor.
Tiberius and Gaius Gracchus, brothers who tried to give land to poor citizens and were killed in political violence; Plutarch pairs them with two reforming kings of Sparta.
Cicero, the orator, who spoke for the Republic and was killed in the proscriptions after Caesar’s death.
Antony, Caesar’s friend, whose alliance with Cleopatra ended in defeat at Actium in 31 BC. Plutarch offers his life, with that of Demetrius, as a warning.

full.html: Thinking Plutarch takes sides like a party writer. He admires Cato the Younger and Brutus for their principles, but he also praises Caesar’s mercy to his enemies and blames the violence on all sides. His judgments are moral (was this man brave, honest, self-controlled?) rather than political.

items: Shakespeare built Julius Caesar, Antony and Cleopatra and Coriolanus on North’s Plutarch. The soothsayer’s warning comes straight from the Life of Caesar.
Words and phrases like “the die is cast” (Caesar at the Rubicon) and “veni, vidi, vici” reached us largely through Plutarch and the Roman biographer Suetonius.
Republics: later readers studied these lives to learn how a free government can fall into one-man rule.

deep.text: Context: looking back on the Republic

deep.html: Plutarch wrote under emperors such as Trajan, more than a century after the Republic fell. He could look back calmly on its last generation and ask what in each man’s character led to the civil wars. He used many sources, some now lost, including Cicero’s own writings and Caesar’s accounts of his wars.

items: Is ambition, like Caesar’s wish to be first, a virtue or a danger? When does it become one or the other?
Coriolanus turned back for his mother’s sake. What makes a person listen when nothing else works?
Can a good person do a wrong thing for a good reason? How does Plutarch judge Brutus?
Why might it help to read about one event, like Caesar’s death, from several people’s points of view?

deep.html: Tacitus, the next rung, tells what happened after the Republic: the rule of the first emperors, seen through a senator’s eyes. Shakespeare turned Plutarch’s Romans into plays. Machiavelli, Montesquieu and Rousseau, later on this ladder, all drew lessons about republics from these same Roman lives.

questions: Caesar told the pirates he was worth more ransom. Was that brave, proud, or both?
“I had rather be the first man among these fellows than the second man in Rome.” Would you rather be first in a small place or second in a big one? Why?
Coriolanus’s mother changed his mind when no one else could. Who can change your mind?
Cato lived plainly though he was important. Does having more make it harder to live well?
Plutarch tells Caesar’s death from several sides. Why might that be fairer than one account?
